title: The Ninth of Av
lead: The Jewish day of fasting and mourning for the destruction of the two temples, the fifth-month fast of Zechariah's day, on which the Book of Lamentations is read.

sections.b: Second Kings 25:8 gives the seventh day of the fifth month for the arrival of Nebuzaradan to burn the city; Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth. Zechariah speaks of a fast in the fifth month that the people had kept for seventy years (Zechariah 7:3-5) and promises that the fasts will become feasts (Zechariah 8:19). The rabbis settled the date as the ninth (Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6; Bavli Ta'anit 29a records the discussion of the ninth and tenth). Josephus puts the burning of the second temple on the tenth of the month he calls Loos (War 6.4.5).

The Mishnah lists five things that happened on the ninth of Av: the decree that the generation of the exodus would die in the wilderness (the spies' report, Numbers 14), the destruction of the first and the second temples, the fall of Betar, and the plowing of the city. These are rabbinic traditions, not statements of the Bible.

Lamentations is read in the evening in a synagogue with dimmed lights, in a low voice, with the congregation seated low or on the floor. Later poems called kinot (elegies) are added. The reader repeats Lamentations 5:21 after 5:22 so the scroll does not end on a sad word. Christian Tenebrae, which uses Lamentations in Holy Week, is a separate custom with a different meaning.
